blocks.body:
The Riemann integral handles continuous functions well and limits badly. List the rationals in $[0, 1]$ as $q_1, q_2, q_3, \dots$ and let $f_n$ be $1$ at $q_1, \dots, q_n$ and $0$ elsewhere. Each $f_n$ differs from $0$ at finitely many points, so it is Riemann integrable with $\int_0^1 f_n = 0$ ([[riemann-integral]]). But $f_n$ increases pointwise to the Dirichlet function $\mathbf 1_{\mathbb Q}$ (equal to $1$ on rationals and $0$ on irrationals), which is not Riemann integrable at all: every upper sum is $1$ and every lower sum is $0$. An increasing sequence of integrable functions, all bounded by $1$, has a limit the theory cannot integrate.

Lebesgue's remedy (in his thesis of 1902) has two parts. First, assign a size to far more general sets than intervals. Second, integrate by grouping points according to the value of $f$ rather than their position: instead of cutting the $x$-axis into intervals, cut the $y$-axis and ask how large each set $\{x : f(x) > t\}$ is. This lesson builds both parts on $\mathbb R$ and then turns to the convergence theorems.

blocks.title: Measuring sets: outer measure
blocks.body:
We would like a size $m(A) \in [0, \infty]$ for subsets $A \subseteq \mathbb R$ with $m([a, b]) = b - a$, invariance under translation, and countable additivity: $m(\bigcup_k A_k) = \sum_k m(A_k)$ for pairwise disjoint $A_1, A_2, \dots$. Countable additivity, not just finite additivity, is what will make limits work.

The natural first attempt is to cover $A$ by intervals as economically as possible. For an interval $I$ let $\ell(I)$ be its length, and define the Lebesgue outer measure
$$m^*(A) = \inf\Big\{ \sum_{k=1}^\infty \ell(I_k) : A \subseteq \bigcup_{k=1}^\infty I_k,\ I_k \text{ open intervals} \Big\}.$$
Clearly $m^*$ is monotone ($A \subseteq B$ implies $m^*(A) \le m^*(B)$) and translation invariant. It is also countably subadditive, $m^*(\bigcup_k A_k) \le \sum_k m^*(A_k)$: if the right side is finite and $\varepsilon > 0$, cover each $A_k$ by intervals of total length at most $m^*(A_k) + \varepsilon/2^k$; all these intervals together cover the union and have total length at most $\sum_k m^*(A_k) + \varepsilon$.

Countable sets have outer measure $0$. If $A = \{a_1, a_2, \dots\}$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, cover $a_k$ by an open interval of length $\varepsilon/2^k$; the total length is $\sum_k \varepsilon/2^k = \varepsilon$. So $m^*(\mathbb Q) = 0$, although $\mathbb Q$ is dense. A set of outer measure $0$ is called null, and a property that holds outside a null set is said to hold almost everywhere (a.e.).

blocks.title: The outer measure of an interval is its length

blocks.body:
The single interval $(a - \varepsilon, b + \varepsilon)$ covers $[a, b]$, so $m^*([a, b]) \le b - a + 2\varepsilon$ for every $\varepsilon > 0$, hence $m^*([a,b]) \le b - a$.

For the reverse inequality, let $(I_k)$ be a countable cover of $[a, b]$ by open intervals. Since $[a, b]$ is compact (Heine–Borel, see [[compactness]]), finitely many of the $I_k$ already cover it, so it suffices to show that every finite cover of $[a, b]$ by open intervals has total length greater than $b - a$.

Choose an interval $(a_1, b_1)$ of the cover containing $a$. If $b_1 > b$, stop. Otherwise $b_1 \in [a, b]$, so some interval $(a_2, b_2)$ of the cover contains $b_1$, and $a_2 < b_1 < b_2$. Continue: while $b_j \le b$, choose an interval $(a_{j+1}, b_{j+1})$ of the cover containing $b_j$. The intervals chosen before step $j + 1$ have right endpoints at most $b_j$, so they do not contain $b_j$; thus no interval is chosen twice, and since the cover is finite the process stops at some $m$ with $b_m > b$. Using $a_1 < a$ and $a_{j+1} < b_j$,
$$\sum_{j=1}^m (b_j - a_j) > (b_1 - a) + \sum_{j=1}^{m-1}(b_{j+1} - b_j) = b_m - a > b - a.$$
The cover contains these $m$ intervals, so its total length is also greater than $b - a$. Taking the infimum over covers, $m^*([a, b]) \ge b - a$.

Compactness is what stops the $\varepsilon/2^k$ trick, which works for the rationals, from shrinking a whole interval.

blocks.title: Measure space
blocks.body:
A $\sigma$-algebra on a set $X$ is a collection $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $X$ that contains $X$ and is closed under complements and countable unions (hence also countable intersections). A measure on $\mathcal F$ is a function $\mu : \mathcal F \to [0, \infty]$ with $\mu(\varnothing) = 0$ that is countably additive: $\mu(\bigcup_k E_k) = \sum_k \mu(E_k)$ for pairwise disjoint $E_k \in \mathcal F$. The triple $(X, \mathcal F, \mu)$ is a measure space; when $\mu(X) = 1$ it is a probability space. A null set is a set in $\mathcal F$ of measure $0$, and almost everywhere means outside some null set.

So a measure is a consistent way of assigning sizes to the sets in $\mathcal F$, additive over countable disjoint unions.

blocks.title: Measurable sets and Lebesgue measure
blocks.body:
Outer measure is defined on every subset of $\mathbb R$, but it is not countably additive on all of them. In fact no function on all subsets of $\mathbb R$ has the three desired properties. Vitali (1905) used the axiom of choice to build a set $V \subseteq [0, 1]$ whose translates $V + q$, for the rationals $q \in [-1, 1]$, are pairwise disjoint and have a union that contains $[0, 1]$ and lies inside $[-1, 2]$. Countable additivity and translation invariance would make the size of that union a sum of countably many copies of the size of $V$, which is $0$ or $\infty$, never a number in $[1, 3]$.

So we restrict to well-behaved sets. Carathéodory's criterion: a set $E \subseteq \mathbb R$ is Lebesgue measurable if
$$m^*(A) = m^*(A \cap E) + m^*(A \setminus E) \quad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb R,$$
that is, $E$ splits every set additively. The central theorem of the construction, proved in all the references, is: the Lebesgue measurable sets form a $\sigma$-algebra containing every interval, hence every open set and every closed set; and on this $\sigma$-algebra $m = m^*$ is a measure. This $m$ is Lebesgue measure. Every null set is measurable, in particular every countable set.

blocks.title: Measurable functions and the Lebesgue integral
blocks.body:
Let $(X, \mathcal F, \mu)$ be a measure space. A function $f : X \to [-\infty, \infty]$ is measurable if $\{x : f(x) > t\} \in \mathcal F$ for every real $t$.

A simple function is a finite combination $s = \sum_{i=1}^k c_i\mathbf 1_{E_i}$ with $c_i \ge 0$ and $E_i \in \mathcal F$; its integral is $\int s\,d\mu = \sum_i c_i\,\mu(E_i)$, with the convention $0 \cdot \infty = 0$. For measurable $f \ge 0$,
$$\int f\,d\mu = \sup\Big\{ \int s\,d\mu : 0 \le s \le f,\ s \text{ simple} \Big\} \in [0, \infty].$$
A measurable $f$ is integrable if $\int |f|\,d\mu < \infty$, and then $\int f\,d\mu = \int f^+\,d\mu - \int f^-\,d\mu$, where $f^+ = \max(f, 0)$ and $f^- = \max(-f, 0)$.

So the integral of a nonnegative function is approximated from below by functions with finitely many values, each value weighted by the measure of the set where it is taken.

blocks.title: Slicing the range
blocks.body:
Lebesgue's picture: to integrate $f \ge 0$, cut the $y$-axis into levels and approximate $f$ on each set $\{y_i \le f < y_{i+1}\}$ by the lower level $y_i$. The standard choice is
$$s_n = \sum_{i=0}^{n2^n - 1}\frac{i}{2^n}\,\mathbf 1_{\{i/2^n \le f < (i+1)/2^n\}} + n\,\mathbf 1_{\{f \ge n\}},$$
a sequence of simple functions that increases pointwise to $f$. The sets involved may be as irregular as you like, which is why measurability is required and why no continuity is needed. Adding up over levels gives the layer-cake formula
$$\int f\,d\mu = \int_0^\infty \mu(\{x : f(x) > t\})\,dt \qquad (f \ge 0 \text{ measurable}).$$
For instance, with $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0, 1]$ and $0 \le t < 1$, the set $\{f > t\} = (\sqrt t, 1]$ has measure $1 - \sqrt t$, and $\int_0^1 (1 - \sqrt t)\,dt = 1 - \frac23 = \frac13$, as it should be.

The new integral extends the old one: every Riemann integrable function on $[a, b]$ is Lebesgue integrable, with the same integral. Lebesgue also characterised Riemann integrability: a bounded function on $[a, b]$ is Riemann integrable if and only if its set of discontinuity points is null. The Dirichlet function is discontinuous everywhere and fails; its Lebesgue integral is simply $1 \cdot m(\mathbb Q \cap [0, 1]) = 0$.

blocks.title: Monotone convergence and Fatou's lemma
blocks.body:
Let $f_1, f_2, \dots$ be measurable functions on a measure space $(X, \mathcal F, \mu)$ with values in $[0, \infty]$.
1. Monotone convergence theorem: if $f_1 \le f_2 \le \cdots$ and $f_n \to f$ pointwise, then $f$ is measurable and $\int f_n\,d\mu \to \int f\,d\mu$.
2. Fatou's lemma: $\liminf_n f_n$ is measurable and $\displaystyle\int \liminf_{n\to\infty} f_n\,d\mu \le \liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu$.

blocks.title: Where these come from
blocks.body:
The proof of the monotone convergence theorem combines the definition of the integral as a supremum over simple functions with the countable additivity of $\mu$; see Folland, Chapter 2. Fatou's lemma then follows in a few lines. Put $g_n = \inf_{k \ge n} f_k$. These functions are measurable and nonnegative, they increase with $n$, and their limit is $\liminf_k f_k$. Since $g_n \le f_k$ for every $k \ge n$, we have $\int g_n\,d\mu \le \inf_{k \ge n}\int f_k\,d\mu$. Now let $n \to \infty$: by monotone convergence the left side tends to $\int \liminf_k f_k\,d\mu$, and the right side tends to $\liminf_k \int f_k\,d\mu$.

Applied to the opening example, monotone convergence gives $\int_0^1 \mathbf 1_{\mathbb Q}\,dm = \lim \int f_n\,dm = 0$: the limit that the Riemann theory could not handle is now automatic.

blocks.title: Dominated convergence theorem
blocks.body:
Let $f_n$ and $f$ be measurable, with $f_n \to f$ almost everywhere, and suppose there is an integrable function $g$ with $|f_n| \le g$ almost everywhere for every $n$. Then $f$ is integrable and
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu = \int f\,d\mu.$$

First we make the hypotheses hold everywhere. Since $g$ is integrable, $g < \infty$ almost everywhere. Let $N$ be the set of points where $f_n(x)$ does not converge to $f(x)$, or $|f_n(x)| > g(x)$ for some $n$, or $g(x) = \infty$. It is contained in a countable union of null sets, so it is null. Redefining $f_n$, $f$ and $g$ to be $0$ on $N$ changes no integral, so we may assume that $f_n \to f$ and $|f_n| \le g < \infty$ everywhere. Then $|f| \le g$, so $f$ and every $f_n$ are integrable.

The functions $g + f_n$ and $g - f_n$ are measurable and nonnegative, and they converge to $g + f$ and $g - f$. By Fatou's lemma and linearity of the integral on integrable functions,
$$\int g + \int f = \int (g + f) \le \liminf_n \int (g + f_n) = \int g + \liminf_n \int f_n,$$
$$\int g - \int f = \int (g - f) \le \liminf_n \int (g - f_n) = \int g - \limsup_n \int f_n,$$
where the last step uses $\liminf_n (-a_n) = -\limsup_n a_n$. Since $\int g$ is finite we may cancel it, which gives $\limsup_n \int f_n \le \int f \le \liminf_n \int f_n$. Hence $\lim_n \int f_n$ exists and equals $\int f$.

blocks.title: An uncountable null set
blocks.body: Let $E$ be the set of numbers in $[0, 1]$ that have a decimal expansion using no digit $7$. Show that $m(E) = 0$, although $E$ is uncountable.
blocks.solution:
Fix $k$. If $x \in E$, the first $k$ digits $d_1, \dots, d_k$ of such an expansion avoid $7$, and $x$ lies in the closed interval $[0.d_1 \ldots d_k,\ 0.d_1 \ldots d_k + 10^{-k}]$. There are $9^k$ choices for the digits, so $E$ is covered by $9^k$ intervals of length $10^{-k}$ and
$$m^*(E) \le 9^k \cdot 10^{-k} = (0.9)^k.$$
(Closed intervals are harmless: enlarging each to an open interval adds as little total length as we like.) This holds for every $k$ and $(0.9)^k \to 0$, so $m^*(E) = 0$.

$E$ is uncountable: it contains every number $0.d_1d_2d_3\ldots$ with all $d_i \in \{0, 1\}$. Different such digit strings give different numbers, because a number with two decimal expansions has one ending in $000\ldots$ and the other in $999\ldots$, and by Cantor's diagonal argument there are uncountably many such strings.

So null does not mean countable. Also, almost every $x \in [0, 1]$ has a $7$ in its decimal expansion, and since a countable union of null sets is null, almost every $x$ uses all ten digits. Much more is true: by Borel's normal number theorem, for almost every $x$ each digit appears with limiting frequency $\frac1{10}$.

blocks.title: When domination fails
blocks.body: Let $f_n = n\,\mathbf 1_{(0, 1/n)}$ on $[0, 1]$. Find $\lim f_n$ and $\lim \int f_n\,dm$, and explain which hypothesis of the dominated convergence theorem fails.
blocks.solution:
$f_n(0) = 0$, and for $x > 0$, $f_n(x) = 0$ as soon as $n \ge 1/x$. So $f_n \to 0$ everywhere, while $\int f_n = n \cdot \frac1n = 1$ for every $n$. The limit of the integrals is $1$ and the integral of the limit is $0$; Fatou's inequality $0 \le 1$ is strict.

A dominating function would have to satisfy $g \ge \sup_n f_n$. For $x \in [\frac{1}{k+1}, \frac1k)$, $f_n(x) = n$ exactly when $n < 1/x$, that is, for $n \le k$; so $\sup_n f_n = k$ there, and
$$\int_0^1 \sup_n f_n\,dm = \sum_{k=1}^\infty k\Big(\frac1k - \frac{1}{k+1}\Big) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{k+1} = \infty.$$
No integrable $g$ dominates the sequence. The unit of mass escapes into an ever narrower spike.

blocks.title: Dominated convergence at work
blocks.body: Compute $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^n \Big(1 - \frac xn\Big)^n dx$ in two ways: directly, and by dominated convergence.
blocks.solution:
Directly: substituting $u = 1 - x/n$,
$$\int_0^n \Big(1 - \frac xn\Big)^n dx = n\int_0^1 u^n\,du = \frac{n}{n + 1} \to 1.$$
By dominated convergence, which is how one argues when no antiderivative is available: on $[0, \infty)$ let $f_n(x) = (1 - x/n)^n$ for $0 \le x \le n$ and $f_n(x) = 0$ for $x > n$. For fixed $x$, once $n > x$ we have $f_n(x) = (1 - x/n)^n \to e^{-x}$. The inequality $1 - t \le e^{-t}$, valid for all real $t$ because the convex function $e^{-t}$ lies above its tangent line at $0$, gives $0 \le 1 - x/n \le e^{-x/n}$ on $[0, n]$, and raising to the $n$-th power, $0 \le f_n(x) \le e^{-x}$. As $\int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx = 1 < \infty$, dominated convergence gives
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^\infty f_n\,dm = \int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx = 1.$$
Now fix $s > 0$. Multiplying the same bound by $x^{s-1}$ gives $0 \le f_n(x)x^{s-1} \le e^{-x}x^{s-1}$ on $(0, \infty)$, and $e^{-x}x^{s-1}$ is integrable there because $s > 0$. So dominated convergence gives $\int_0^n (1 - x/n)^n x^{s-1}\,dx \to \int_0^\infty e^{-x}x^{s-1}\,dx = \Gamma(s)$. Integrating by parts $n$ times, the left side equals $\dfrac{n!\,n^s}{s(s+1)\cdots(s+n)}$, and this proves Gauss's product formula
$$\Gamma(s) = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n!\,n^s}{s(s+1)\cdots(s+n)} \qquad (s > 0)$$
for the [[gamma]] function.

blocks.body:
- Not every subset of $\mathbb R$ is measurable (Vitali's set needs the axiom of choice), but every Borel set is (a set in the smallest $\sigma$-algebra containing the intervals).
- The Lebesgue integral is absolutely convergent by definition. $\int_0^\infty \frac{\sin x}{x}\,dx = \frac\pi2$ exists as an improper Riemann integral ([[improper-integrals]]), but $\int_0^\infty \frac{|\sin x|}{x}\,dx = \infty$ (the part over $[k\pi, (k+1)\pi]$ is at least $\frac{2}{(k+1)\pi}$), so $\frac{\sin x}{x}$ is not Lebesgue integrable on $[0, \infty)$.
- Pointwise or almost-everywhere convergence alone never justifies $\int \lim = \lim \int$; you need monotonicity, an integrable dominating function, or some other argument. On a set of infinite measure even uniform convergence is not enough: $\frac1n\mathbf 1_{[0, n]} \to 0$ uniformly on $\mathbb R$, with integral $1$ for every $n$.
- Fatou's lemma is an inequality in one direction only, and it needs $f_n \ge 0$ (or a lower bound by a fixed integrable function).

In probability, a random variable is a measurable function on a probability space and its expectation is its Lebesgue integral. Monotone and dominated convergence are used constantly in [[random-variables]] and [[limit-theorems]], and the strong law of large numbers is a statement about almost-everywhere convergence ([[probability-basics]]). The spaces $L^p$ of functions with $\int |f|^p < \infty$ (functions equal a.e. being identified) are complete; for $p = 2$ this is the Riesz–Fischer theorem, the foundation of the $L^2$ theory of [[fourier-poisson|Fourier series]].

Dominated convergence generalises the interchange theorem of [[uniform-convergence]]: on $[a, b]$ a uniformly convergent sequence of bounded functions is eventually dominated by a constant. It also justifies differentiating under the integral sign and many manipulations with [[improper-integrals]]. In number theory, 'almost all' statements about real numbers, such as the metric theory of [[continued-fractions]] and Khinchin's theorem in [[diophantine-approx|Diophantine approximation]], are statements about Lebesgue measure.

1. Show that the Cantor set (remove the open middle third of $[0, 1]$, then the open middle thirds of the two remaining intervals, and so on) is null, by computing the total length removed.
2. Use countable subadditivity and $m^*([0, 1]) = 1$ to show that $[0, 1]$ is uncountable.
3. Use dominated convergence to find $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^\infty \frac{n\sin(x/n)}{x(1 + x^2)}\,dx$.
4. Let $f_n = \mathbf 1_{[n, n+1]}$ on $\mathbb R$. Show that $f_n \to 0$ pointwise, compute $\int f_n\,dm$, and say which hypothesis of the dominated convergence theorem fails.
